passage: Arnab, you asked why I get upset when people say "these migrants." Let me tell you about Zainab. When I was your age, she joined our school in Kolkata. Her family had come from across the border after floods took their fields. The other kids called her names. I didn't join in, but I didn't stop them either. One day we had a geography project on rivers, and she was put in my group. She knew everything about how the delta shifts, how floods move people. She told us about her grandfather's boat. I realised I'd been scared of her without knowing anything. After that I asked her questions. We're still friends. So when you hear "these migrants," ask who they are first.

qa.q: What had taken Zainab's family's fields?
qa.a: Floods had taken their fields.

qa.q: How did the speaker feel about Zainab before the geography project?
qa.a: They were scared of her without really knowing her, and felt uneasy about not stopping the name-calling.

qa.q: What advice does the speaker give Arnab, and why is it useful?
qa.a: To ask who migrants are before judging, because curiosity replaces fear and stereotypes with real people's stories.

qa.q: How might Zainab have felt when her classmate started asking questions?
qa.a: She probably felt seen and less alone, after being called names by others.

grounding: An elder uses a memory of a migrant classmate to teach curiosity over prejudice.

passage: Dolma had one week to finish her school project on migration, and the only person she could interview was Yash, the new boy whose family had moved from a town in Nepal. The problem: Yash barely spoke, and the library's internet was down. Dolma waited after class. "Can I ask you some questions? For the project?" Yash looked wary. "Why?" "Because I only know what's in the textbook," she said honestly. He hesitated, then shrugged. For three lunch breaks they sat on the steps. He told her about the long bus journey, missing his grandmother, learning Hindi from cartoons. Dolma realised some classmates' jokes about him were plain cruel. In her presentation, she used his words, with his permission, and the class went quiet.

qa.q: Where did Yash's family move from?
qa.a: They moved from a town in Nepal.

qa.q: Why did Yash look wary at first?
qa.a: He may have expected to be mocked or used, since some classmates had joked about him, so he wasn't sure Dolma's interest was genuine.

qa.q: What helped Dolma get Yash to open up?
qa.a: She was honest about only knowing the textbook and gave him time over three lunch breaks, which showed real curiosity rather than judgement.

qa.q: How might the class see Yash after the presentation?
qa.a: Some may see him as a real person with a story now, and feel uncomfortable about their earlier jokes.

grounding: It shows a teen learning about migration and prejudice through curious, honest conversations with a classmate.

passage: Gargi's colony in Bengaluru had a new family on the third floor, from Afghanistan. Some neighbours whispered at the gate. Gargi's friend Gurleen said her mother had told her to "be careful." Gargi wasn't sure what that meant. At the building's Holi, the new family's daughter stood at the edge with a plate of sweets she had brought. Nobody took one. Gargi walked over and took two. "What are these?" she asked. The girl explained they were from Kabul, made for celebrations. Gurleen came over, a bit slowly, and tried one. "It's like a cousin of our barfi," she said. The girl laughed. Later, Gargi asked her mother why people were whispering. Her mother said, "People fear what they don't know."

qa.q: Where was the new family from?
qa.a: They were from Afghanistan.

qa.q: Why might Gurleen have walked over slowly?
qa.a: She may have felt unsure because of her mother's warning, but curiosity and seeing Gargi go first pulled her in.

qa.q: What did Gargi's choice at Holi do well?
qa.a: By taking the sweets and asking a question, she broke the awkward silence and made space for the new girl to share her culture.

qa.q: What would change if nobody had taken a sweet?
qa.a: The new girl would likely have felt rejected and alone, and the whispers might have hardened into lasting prejudice.

grounding: It shows teens overcoming neighbours' prejudice towards a migrant family through curiosity at a festival.

passage: 'Ammi, for my social studies project, can I interview you?' Noor laughed. 'About what, Hafsa? My cooking?' 'Migration. You moved from Darbhanga to Mumbai, right?' 'When I was nineteen, after marriage. Why?' 'What was it like?' Noor wiped her hands. 'Lonely. People in the building called us “those Biharis”. One aunty wouldn't let her son play with your mamu's children.' Hafsa stopped writing. 'That's awful.' 'It changed slowly. The same aunty later came to me for my litti recipe.' Hafsa thought. 'There's an Afghan boy in my class. Some boys call him “refugee” like it's a bad word.' 'And you?' 'I've never asked him anything.' Noor raised an eyebrow. 'Maybe start with curiosity.'

qa.q: Where did Noor move from, and to where?
qa.a: From Darbhanga to Mumbai.

qa.q: What does Hafsa's pause in writing suggest Hafsa was feeling?
qa.a: Hafsa was shocked and saddened to learn Ammi faced prejudice, and it prompted some thinking.

qa.q: What could Hafsa do next about the Afghan boy in her class?
qa.a: Hafsa could talk to him with genuine curiosity about his story, rather than joining or ignoring the name-calling.

qa.q: How might the Afghan boy feel if someone asked about his life with real interest?
qa.a: He might feel seen as a person rather than a label, and less alone.

grounding: Shows a teen learning about migration and prejudice through curiosity and a family story.

passage: When Sonali joined our class in Delhi last year, I'll be honest, I had made up my mind about her before she even spoke. Her family had come from Nepal, and I'd seen videos that said migrants take jobs and don't belong. I didn't say anything mean, I just didn't talk to her. Then we were paired for a geography project on the Himalayas. She knew the names of rivers I couldn't even spell. She told me her father walked for two days to reach the bus that would bring them here. I asked a hundred questions after that. I was curious for the first time, not suspicious. I'm Mehak, sixteen. It scares me a little how easily those videos had shaped me.

qa.q: What was Mehak and Sonali's geography project about?
qa.a: The Himalayas.

qa.q: Why does it scare Mehak how easily the videos shaped Mehak?
qa.a: Mehak feels uneasy on realising Sonali had been judged without being known, simply from what Mehak had watched.

qa.q: What changed Mehak's attitude toward Sonali?
qa.a: Working together and asking genuine questions about Sonali's life replaced Mehak's assumptions with real knowledge.

qa.q: How might Sonali have experienced Mehak's silence in the first weeks?
qa.a: She probably felt excluded or unwelcome, not knowing why Mehak kept away.

grounding: A teen reflects on replacing prejudice about migrants with curiosity and understanding.

passage: Class 9 social science, project week. Kavitha chose "a family that moved" for her oral history and asked Hafsa, new this year, for an interview. Hafsa agreed only after reading the questions first. Kavitha asked why the family left their town in eastern Uttar Pradesh, what her father missed, what surprised them in Pune. In the presentation she quoted Hafsa: "On the first day, someone asked if we had electricity back home." A few students laughed. Kavitha paused, then said, "My Nani's village loses power most evenings. Nobody laughs at her." The room went quiet. Afterwards two boys asked Hafsa about her town's winter fair. I plan to make oral histories a full unit next term, and I will speak privately with the students who laughed. — Mr Pillai

qa.q: Which city did Hafsa's family move to?
qa.a: Pune.

qa.q: What does Kavitha's pause during the presentation suggest?
qa.a: Kavitha seems uncomfortable with the laughter and protective of Hafsa, choosing a calm reply from her own family's life instead of an angry one.

qa.q: What could Mr Pillai do next, beyond the plans in the note?
qa.a: Mr Pillai could let students like Hafsa choose what to share, and discuss common stereotypes openly so the laughter is understood, not just stopped.

qa.q: How might the interview have felt for Hafsa?
qa.a: Hafsa was cautious at first, but being asked real questions about home, and later about the winter fair, probably felt respectful and welcoming.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a student's curious oral history of a migrant classmate turning a prejudiced laugh into interest.

passage:
Thursday, 9:40 pm
New girl in section B, Sabina. Grew up in Nairobi, her family's Gujarati, and she speaks Swahili with her brother when she's annoyed 😅 At lunch Megha asked if she'd lived "with lions" and everyone laughed. I laughed too. Then Sabina said, flat, "We had traffic jams and a school canteen," and I wanted to vanish. So in bio I asked her real things. Why did her great-grandfather go to Kenya at all? (Railway work, about a hundred years back.) Why come back now? (Her mum's job.) What does she miss? (Mandazi, and rain on tin roofs.) I didn't know half of this history. Tomorrow I'm taking her the library book on Indian families in East Africa, and saying sorry for the lion laugh.
— Parul

qa.q: Where did Sabina grow up?
qa.a: In Nairobi.

qa.q: How did Parul feel after Sabina's flat reply about traffic jams?
qa.a: Parul felt ashamed of laughing and wanted to vanish, and that discomfort turned into curiosity about Sabina's real story.

qa.q: What small step is Parul planning, and why might it help?
qa.a: Bringing the library book and apologising for the lion laugh shows Sabina respect and keeps the curious conversation going.

qa.q: What is it like for Sabina when the table laughs about lions?
qa.a: Sabina probably feels tired and hurt at being reduced to a stereotype, which is why her reply comes out flat.

grounding: A diary shows a teenager moving from laughing at a stereotype to curious questions about a classmate's migration history.

passage:
In their Kerala village, new families had arrived from Bihar to work at the brick kiln. Some people at the tea shop grumbled. "They'll take our jobs."
Vandana heard her friend Madhav say, "They don't even speak Malayalam."
One Sunday, Vandana went with her mother to the kiln to give old clothes. A girl her age, Pinky, was teaching her little brother the alphabet on a slate.
They talked in broken Hindi and hand signs. Pinky's father had left their village after the floods destroyed their field.
On the way home, Vandana said to Madhav, "They didn't come to take anything. Their farm drowned."
Madhav was quiet. "I didn't know that."
The next week, they both went to help at the kiln school.

qa.q: Why had Pinky's father left their village?
qa.a: The floods destroyed their field.

qa.q: What was Madhav feeling when he said "I didn't know that"?
qa.a: Madhav felt surprised and a little ashamed of his earlier comment.

qa.q: What did Vandana do that others in the village could learn from?
qa.a: She met the migrant family, listened to their story, and shared it, replacing rumours with understanding.

qa.q: How might Pinky see Vandana's visits?
qa.a: Pinky probably feels welcomed and less like an outsider.

grounding: A village teen learns a migrant family's story and challenges local prejudice.

passage:
In Berlin, Alejandro and Zeynep had to interview someone for a school project on migration.
Alejandro's family had come from Colombia five years ago. Zeynep's grandparents had come from Turkey in the 1970s.
"Let's interview your grandmother," Alejandro said.
Zeynep's grandmother spoke slowly in German, switching to Turkish when she got emotional. She told them about arriving with one suitcase, working in a factory, and people shouting "Go home!" on the tram.
Alejandro swallowed. Someone had said that to his father last month.
On the way back, Zeynep said, "I never asked her before."
Alejandro said, "I'm going to ask my dad tonight."

qa.q: Where had Zeynep's grandparents come from?
qa.a: From Turkey.

qa.q: What was Alejandro feeling when he swallowed?
qa.a: Alejandro felt moved and hurt, connecting her story to what happened to his father.

qa.q: What could Alejandro and Zeynep do with these stories?
qa.a: Include both family stories in their project so classmates understand migration and prejudice personally.

qa.q: How might Zeynep's grandmother feel being asked about her past?
qa.a: She likely feels valued and emotional, sharing memories she hadn't told before.

grounding: Two teens in Germany learn migration stories from family members through a school project.

passage:
A new student joined Class 10 in the Delhi school. Samir had come from Afghanistan with his family a year ago.
At lunch, some students asked him, "Did you see bombs?" Samir went quiet.
Rehana, who was curious too, asked something different. "What food do you miss most?"
Samir's face softened. "My mother's bolani. And the mulberries from our garden."
"What's bolani?"
He drew it on a napkin: a stuffed flatbread. Rehana said her Nani made something similar with potatoes.
The next week, Samir brought bolani for the class. Rehana brought her Nani's aloo paratha. They compared.

qa.q: What food does Samir miss most?
qa.a: His mother's bolani, and the mulberries from their garden.

qa.q: What was Samir feeling when he went quiet after the question about bombs?
qa.a: Samir felt uncomfortable and hurt, as if his whole identity was reduced to war.

qa.q: What did Rehana's different question do?
qa.a: It showed curiosity about Samir's life and culture, which opened up a real conversation.

qa.q: How might the students who asked about bombs see things after the food exchange?
qa.a: They might start seeing Samir as a person with a rich life, not just a story of war.

grounding: A teen welcomes a migrant classmate through curious, respectful questions.

passage:
Dear Salma,
Remember in Class 8, when you joined our school, I asked if people in Afghanistan lived in tents? You said, "Some do. My family had a flat with a balcony and a lemon tree," and walked off. I thought you were rude.
This term, for our geography project, I read about why families leave their countries: war, work, danger. I watched an interview with a girl who had to leave her school behind. I thought about you, and the lemon tree.
I'm sorry for that question. I wasn't trying to be mean, but I only knew one picture.
I'd really like to hear about your city, if you want to tell me. What did your old street sound like in the morning? And do you miss the lemons?
From your old bench partner,
Akash

qa.q: What did Salma's family have at their flat?
qa.a: A balcony and a lemon tree.

qa.q: How does Akash feel now about the Class 8 question?
qa.a: Akash feels sorry and a bit ashamed, realising it came from knowing only one picture of Afghanistan.

qa.q: What would you advise Akash while waiting for Salma's reply?
qa.a: Be patient, listen without assumptions, and accept whatever Salma chooses to share, or not.

qa.q: How might Salma have felt when Akash asked about tents?
qa.a: Salma probably felt hurt and misunderstood, seen only as a stereotype instead of a person with a home.

grounding: Illustrates a teen using curiosity and learning about migration to understand an old prejudice and apologise.

passage:
Lokesh, on your podcast you asked what changed my mind about migrants. It was my own Uppa.
I'm Nazia. My grandfather went from Kozhikode to Dubai at nineteen to work on building sites. I'd heard the family version: brave, successful, sent money home. But at school, I'd also laughed at jokes about the workers who come to our city from Bihar and Odisha.
For a school project I interviewed three of them at a construction site near our flat. One man, Manoj, showed me a photo of his daughter's school uniform. He said he sees her once a year.
That night I asked Uppa what Dubai was like. He was quiet, then said, "Lonely. People called us names." I realised the men I'd laughed at were living his story.
I don't laugh at those jokes anymore. I ask where people are from instead.

qa.q: Where did Nazia's grandfather go to work at nineteen?
qa.a: He went from Kozhikode to Dubai to work on building sites.

qa.q: How did Nazia feel after Uppa said Dubai was lonely?
qa.a: Nazia felt shaken and ashamed, realising the workers Nazia had laughed at were living Uppa's story.

qa.q: What could other students learn from Nazia's project?
qa.a: Talking to people directly and connecting their stories to your own family can break down prejudice more than jokes or assumptions.

qa.q: How might Manoj have felt being interviewed by a curious teenager?
qa.a: Manoj may have felt respected and seen, sharing something personal like his daughter's photo.

grounding: Shows a teen understanding migration and a personal prejudice through curiosity about workers' and her family's stories.

passage:
I'm Wasim, and I sit two rows behind Vaibhav in our Bengaluru school.
When the two exchange students from Kenya arrived in November, Vaibhav whispered a joke about lions and running. Some of us laughed. I did too, I'm not proud of it.
Then in geography, the teacher asked them to present their city, Nairobi. They showed photos: tall buildings, traffic jams worse than ours, a mall, their school robotics lab. Vaibhav went very still.
At lunch he walked straight to their table. I couldn't hear everything, but he was asking questions, lots of them, about their school, their food, their music. By Friday he was learning a Swahili greeting.
I don't know if he felt ashamed. He never mentioned the joke. But he never made another one like it.

qa.q: Which city did the exchange students present?
qa.a: Nairobi.

qa.q: What does Vaibhav going very still during the photos suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Vaibhav felt surprised and perhaps ashamed, as the photos showed how wrong his joke's picture was.

qa.q: What would help a class welcome exchange students better from the start?
qa.a: Inviting them to share about their home early, and teachers calmly addressing stereotype jokes, would build curiosity instead of prejudice.

qa.q: How might the exchange students have felt when Vaibhav came to their table?
qa.a: They may have felt cautious at first but pleased that someone was genuinely curious about their lives.

grounding: Illustrates, through an observer, a teen moving from a prejudiced joke to curiosity about another society.

passage:
Monday: At the bus stop, Vidya's friend grumbled that "people from outside" were crowding the city. Vidya nodded, not really thinking about it.
Thursday: For a social-science project on migration, she sat on the building steps with Gautam, the night watchman, and asked why he had left his village in Bihar. He talked about a flooded field, two younger sisters still in school, and his first winter sleeping on a relative's floor. She wrote until her pen ran dry, then asked what he missed most. "My mother's voice in the morning," he said.
The next Tuesday: She presented his story, with his permission, beside a map showing how people have always moved for work. At the bus stop that evening, the same grumble came. Vidya asked, "Do you know anyone who actually moved here?" Her friend went quiet, then said, "My own grandfather, actually."

qa.q: Where did Gautam live before he came to the city?
qa.a: He left his village in Bihar.

qa.q: What does Vidya's question at the bus stop suggest about how her thinking changed?
qa.a: She now feels curious and a little uncomfortable with the easy grumble, and wants her friend to picture real people like Gautam instead of faceless outsiders.

qa.q: Which choice helped Vidya understand migration better, and why?
qa.a: Sitting down to listen to Gautam and asking open questions, like what he missed, turned a vague idea into one person's real reasons and feelings.

qa.q: What might it mean to Gautam that a student asked about his story?
qa.a: He might feel respected and seen, since he shared personal memories and agreed to let her present them.

grounding: Shows a teen's curiosity about a migrant's story softening a prejudiced remark over several days.
